culture_note: Getting someone's attention: a Deaf person can't hear you call their name, so tap them lightly on the shoulder, wave where they can see you, or flick the lights in a room. Then keep eye contact. Looking away while someone signs is like walking off mid-sentence.

Your face is part of the sign. In sign languages, eyebrows, head movements and mouth shapes carry grammar, not just mood. A head shake can turn a sentence into "no", and the same hands with a different face can mean something else. So don't keep a blank face when you practise. Copy the signer's face too.

Many Deaf people see being Deaf as an identity and a community with its own language, not as something missing. "Deaf" (أصم) is the respectful word. Avoid "deaf and dumb" (أطرش، أبكم) and "hearing-impaired". In Deaf communities, people also have a name sign, usually given to them by a Deaf person. You don't make one up for yourself.

Jordanian Sign Language is a full language with its own grammar. It isn't Arabic on the hands, and it isn't universal: it's different from American Sign Language, and even neighbouring Arab countries sign differently. Questions show on the face too: watch the eyebrows in this week's videos.

Most Deaf children (over 90%) are born to hearing parents, and many families never learn to sign. That can leave a Deaf child unable to follow conversations at their own dinner table. A brother, aunt or cousin who learns even a few signs makes a real difference.

Feelings get bigger in sign through the face and the movement. Sign "happy" small with a light smile and it's "a bit happy". Sign it bigger and faster with a big smile and it's "so happy". Try both versions of this week's signs and feel the difference.

When you study or work with a Deaf person through an interpreter, talk to the Deaf person, not the interpreter. Look at them and say "you", not "tell him" or "tell her". In group work, sit in a circle so everyone can see everyone's hands and faces, and take turns instead of talking over each other.

You've finished all eight lessons! The International Day of Sign Languages is 23 September each year, during the International Week of Deaf People. Keep going: look up new words in the Dictionary of Jordanian Sign Language, follow Deaf creators, and practise with a Deaf friend if you can. The review emails will keep coming for a few more weeks.
